title: Astronomers Confirm the Youngest Planet Ever Discovered
summary:
Astronomers have confirmed the youngest planet ever discovered: a world less than 1 million years old, still surrounded by the gas and dust from which it formed. The planet, named Elias 2-24 b, orbits a star about 450 light-years from Earth. It is roughly as massive as Jupiter.

The discovery, published September 16 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, was led by Andrea Bernardi, a doctoral candidate at the Universidad Diego Portales in Chile. The team examined archived observations of seven young stars using the coronagraph at the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. A coronagraph blocks a star's bright light, making it easier to see faint objects nearby.

"The planets should be found within the gaps, since they are carving them," Bernardi said. "And that's exactly where we found Elias 2-24 b."

This finding is significant because most of the roughly 6,000 confirmed exoplanets are billions of years old and orbit close to their stars. They are typically found through transits, which occur when a planet passes in front of its star and causes a small dip in starlight. But transits are hard to detect when planets are still buried in dust or orbit far from their stars.

Elias 2-24 b is different. It is still inside its star's dusty disk, giving scientists a rare chance to study planet formation as it happens. "Our planet-formation models already struggled to explain the previous record holders," said Lucas Cieza, a co-author from the Instituto de Estudios Astrofísicos in Chile. "Elias 2-24 b shows us that even our best planet-formation models are still missing some important processes."

The discovery also resolves a decade-old mystery. Earlier observations from ALMA in Chile revealed a gap in the disk around Elias 2-24. Later, the Very Large Telescope spotted a faint point of light inside that gap. Scientists wondered if it was a planet. The problem: existing theories suggested a large planet should not form so quickly, especially so far from its star. Current models say forming a Jupiter-size planet at Jupiter's distance takes about 5 million years. A giant planet much farther out should take even longer.

"The galaxy churns out new stars and planets continuously, so there are many in every stage of evolution," Cieza said. "That means we can see the entire process in theory, but there is a large gap in what most telescopes can detect. We are mostly blind to these baby planets right now."

Studying this system gives astronomers a glimpse of what our own solar system may have looked like billions of years ago. Future observations will help refine planet-formation models and reveal more about how planets are born.
why_it_matters: A planet younger than any found before shows that the scientific models used to explain how solar systems form are still incomplete — and since those models shape what we expect about where Earth-like worlds can exist, fixing them matters for the search for life beyond our solar system.

background_read: The first planets orbiting other stars — called exoplanets — were confirmed only a few decades ago, and most of the roughly 6,000 known today were found because they briefly dim their star's light. Elias 2-24 b was caught a different way: astronomers used the W. M. Keck Observatory (twin giant telescopes on Mauna Kea, Hawaii) to hunt for faint points of light hidden in the glare of young stars.

The gap in the dust around Elias 2-24 was first spotted by ALMA (the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, a radio telescope on a high plateau in Chile) and later re-examined with the Very Large Telescope (a group of large optical telescopes, also in Chile). Planets are thought to grow inside the disks of gas and dust left over from star formation, sweeping clear lanes as they orbit — exactly the kind of gap seen here.

Andrea Bernardi, who led the study, is a doctoral candidate at the Universidad Diego Portales in Chile, and co-author Lucas Cieza works at the Instituto de Estudios Astrofísicos in the same country. Astronomers care about baby systems like this one because our own solar system — including Jupiter — probably looked similar billions of years ago.

perspectives.description: This is a rare chance to watch planet formation while it is still happening, and it settles a decade-old puzzle about the faint light inside the disk gap. Each baby planet gives researchers fresh data to sharpen their models.

One confirmed object is thin evidence, and the fact that models cannot explain it may mean the models are simply being adjusted to fit each new case. The team itself admits telescopes are 'mostly blind' to baby planets, so the sample is tiny.

Planet hunting has always followed technology: transit surveys delivered thousands of old, close-in planets, while coronagraphs and direct imaging open a different window onto young, distant ones. Every new detection method resets what counts as a record.

Future observations should test whether giant planets can really form quickly so far from their stars, and refine the models that failed here. That work also offers a glimpse of what our own solar system looked like in its first million years.
